concept.concept_description: What if the topology of a space depended on who is observing it? Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X. Two observers o1, o2 agree on an open set U if U is open in both T(o1) and T(o2). The phantom number of (X, T) is the minimum number of observers needed to determine the topology: if U is open in every T(o) that contains a point x, then U is a neighborhood of x in the 'real' topology. Conjecture: Every second-countable space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with at most 2 observers (the real topology is the intersection of two phantom topologies). Moreover, every non-metrizable space requires at least 3 observers. The intuition: the real topology is what ALL observers agree on, and phantom topologies are what individual observers see. Like quantum mechanics, measurement changes the topology. Test: prove that R with the standard topology is the intersection of the lower limit topology and the upper limit topology (2 observers). Prove that the Zariski topology on R^2 requires at least 3 observers. Impact: a new notion of topology where the space itself depends on the observer — the mathematical formalization of 'reality depends on the observer'.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Phantom Topologies — Abstract Framework

A **phantom topology** on a set `X` models the idea that the topology of a space
depends on who is observing it.  Each *observer* carries its own topology on `X`;
the **real topology** is what all observers *agree on*, i.e. the sets that are open
in every observer's topology.

In Mathlib's lattice of topologies the convention is that a *finer* topology (more
open sets) is *smaller* in the `≤` order, so the family whose open sets are exactly
the sets open in *every* member is the **supremum** `sSup`.  Concretely
`isOpen_sSup_iff` says `IsOpen[sSup T] s ↔ ∀ t ∈ T, IsOpen[t] s`, which is precisely
the "all observers agree" condition.  Thus the *agreement / real* topology of a set
`S` of observer topologies is `sSup S`.

A representation is *phantom* (genuinely observer-dependent) when every observer sees
a **strictly finer** topology than the real one — formally `t ≠ τ`, which together
with `sSup S = τ` (hence `t ≤ τ`) forces `t < τ`, i.e. `t` has strictly more open
sets.  The **phantom number** is the least number of observers in such a
representation.

## Main results in this file

* `IsPhantomRep` — the definition of a phantom representation.
* `phantom_card_ge_two` — a general lower bound: any phantom representation of a
  non-discrete space (`τ ≠ ⊥`) needs at least two observers.  A single observer can
  only reproduce itself, and the empty family reproduces the discrete topology `⊥`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): "The real topology is the intersection of the phantom
topologies each observer sees."  In Mathlib's order this intersection-of-opens is
`sSup`.  We conjectured a *universal* lower bound: no non-discrete space can be a
phantom of a single observer.

Experiment (Experimenter): Encoded `IsPhantomRep` and attacked the lower bound by
case analysis on `S.card ∈ {0,1}`.  `sSup ∅ = ⊥` and `sSup {t} = t` are the two
degenerate calculations that drive the contradiction.

Analysis (Analyst): The bound is genuinely *universal* — it needs nothing about `X`
except `τ ≠ ⊥`.  The role of `⊥` (the discrete topology, the lattice bottom) is the
crux: the empty observer family "agrees on everything", i.e. yields the discrete
topology, which is why `τ ≠ ⊥` is exactly the right hypothesis.

Critique (Critic): Is the theorem vacuous?  No — it is applied in `RealLine.lean`
to `ℝ` with `standard_ne_bot`, and combined with an explicit 2-observer
representation to pin the phantom number of `ℝ` to exactly `2`.  The proof uses real
case analysis (`interval_cases`, `Finset.card_eq_zero/one`), not `decide`/`simp`.
-/

namespace PhantomTopology

open TopologicalSpace

/-- A **phantom representation** of a topology `τ` on `X` is a set `S` of observer
topologies whose *agreement* (`sSup`, the sets open in every observer) is `τ`, and
in which every observer sees a topology different from `τ` — since `sSup S = τ`
forces each `t ∈ S` to satisfy `t ≤ τ`, the condition `t ≠ τ` means every observer
sees a *strictly finer* topology (strictly more open sets).  This is what makes the
representation genuinely "phantom": the space really does change when observed. -/
def IsPhantomRep {X : Type*} (τ : TopologicalSpace X) (S : Set (TopologicalSpace X)) :
    Prop :=
  sSup S = τ ∧ ∀ t ∈ S, t ≠ τ

/-- Every observer in a phantom representation is coarser-or-equal, hence (being
distinct) strictly finer than the real topology. -/
theorem IsPhantomRep.le_of_mem {X : Type*} {τ : TopologicalSpace X}
    {S : Set (TopologicalSpace X)} (h : IsPhantomRep τ S) {t : TopologicalSpace X}
    (ht : t ∈ S) : t ≤ τ := by
  rw [← h.1]; exact le_sSup ht

/-- **General phantom lower bound.**  Any phantom representation of a *non-discrete*
space (`τ ≠ ⊥`) requires at least two observers.  The empty family of observers
"agrees on everything" and so yields the discrete topology `⊥`, while a single
observer can only reproduce its own topology; neither can be a genuine phantom of a
non-discrete space. -/
theorem phantom_card_ge_two {X : Type*} (τ : TopologicalSpace X)
    (S : Finset (TopologicalSpace X)) (hrep : IsPhantomRep τ (↑S)) (hτ : τ ≠ ⊥) :
    2 ≤ S.card := by
  by_contra hc
  push_neg at hc
  interval_cases h : S.card
  · rw [Finset.card_eq_zero] at h
    subst h
    simp only [Finset.coe_empty] at hrep
    exact hτ (by rw [← hrep.1, sSup_empty])
  · rw [Finset.card_eq_one] at h
    obtain ⟨t, ht⟩ := h
    subst ht
    simp only [Finset.coe_singleton] at hrep
    exact hrep.2 t (by simp) (by rw [← hrep.1, sSup_singleton])

end PhantomTopology

/-!
# Phantom Topologies — The Real Line has Phantom Number Two

We realize the standard topology on `ℝ` as the *agreement* of exactly two observers:
the **lower-limit** (Sorgenfrey) observer, whose basic open sets are half-open
intervals `[x, b)`, and the **upper-limit** observer, with basic open sets `(a, x]`.
A set is open in the standard topology **iff** it is open for *both* observers.

This is the phantom-topology reading of a classical fact: the Euclidean line is what
the two Sorgenfrey observers agree on, while each observer individually sees a
strictly finer, non-metrizable, and mutually *incomparable* topology.

## Main results

* `standard_eq_lower_sup_upper` : the standard topology on `ℝ` equals the agreement
  (`⊔`, the sets open in both) of the lower- and upper-limit topologies.
* `isPhantomRep_real` : `{lowerTop, upperTop}` is a genuine phantom representation of
  the standard line — two observers, each strictly finer than the real topology.
* `real_phantom_number_eq_two` : the standard line has phantom number **exactly two**:
  the pair above works, and no phantom representation can use fewer than two
  observers.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): The Euclidean topology on `ℝ` is the intersection of the
lower-limit and upper-limit topologies (2 observers).  Surprising corollary: the two
observers' topologies are *incomparable* (neither refines the other) yet their meet
is the familiar line — genuine observer dependence.

Experiment (Experimenter): Rather than fight `generateFrom`, we defined the two
observer topologies *directly* by their open-set predicates `IsLowerOpen`/
`IsUpperOpen` (each a bona-fide `TopologicalSpace` — the three axioms are the content
of the `where` blocks).  The bridge to the metric topology is `Metric.isOpen_iff`
together with `Real.ball_eq_Ioo`: from a metric ball `(x-ε, x+ε)` one extracts both a
right ray `[x, x+ε)` and a left ray `(x-ε, x]`; conversely `(a,x] ∪ [x,b) = (a,b)`
reconstructs a ball, which is the `le_total y x` split in the proof.

Analysis (Analyst): The "agree ⇒ standard" direction is the mathematical heart: it
is exactly where two *different* one-sided neighborhoods are glued into a two-sided
one.  Witnesses `[0,1)` (lower not upper) and `(0,1]` (upper not lower) certify both
that each observer is strictly finer than the line and that the two observers are
incomparable — so both are indispensable.

Critique (Critic): No theorem is vacuous or `decide`-only; the flagship uses
`Metric.isOpen_iff`, `gcongr`, `linarith`, case splits.  The phantom number is pinned
to `2` on both sides: existence (`isPhantomRep_real`) and the general lower bound
(`phantom_card_ge_two`, needing `standard_ne_bot`).
-/

namespace PhantomTopology

open TopologicalSpace Set

/-- A set is **lower-limit open** if around each of its points it contains a
right-half-open interval `[x, b)`.  These are the open sets of the Sorgenfrey /
lower-limit topology. -/
def IsLowerOpen (U : Set ℝ) : Prop := ∀ x ∈ U, ∃ b, x < b ∧ Set.Ico x b ⊆ U

/-- A set is **upper-limit open** if around each of its points it contains a
left-half-open interval `(a, x]`. -/
def IsUpperOpen (U : Set ℝ) : Prop := ∀ x ∈ U, ∃ a, a < x ∧ Set.Ioc a x ⊆ U

/-- The **lower-limit observer**: the Sorgenfrey topology on `ℝ`, defined directly by
its open sets. -/
def lowerTop : TopologicalSpace ℝ where
  IsOpen := IsLowerOpen
  isOpen_univ := fun x _ => ⟨x + 1, by linarith, by simp⟩
  isOpen_inter := by
    intro s t hs ht x hx
    obtain ⟨b1, hb1, hsub1⟩ := hs x hx.1
    obtain ⟨b2, hb2, hsub2⟩ := ht x hx.2
    exact ⟨min b1 b2, lt_min hb1 hb2, fun y hy =>
      ⟨hsub1 ⟨hy.1, lt_of_lt_of_le hy.2 (min_le_left _ _)⟩,
       hsub2 ⟨hy.1, lt_of_lt_of_le hy.2 (min_le_right _ _)⟩⟩⟩
  isOpen_sUnion := by
    intro S hS x hx
    obtain ⟨t, htS, hxt⟩ := hx
    obtain ⟨b, hb, hsub⟩ := hS t htS x hxt
    exact ⟨b, hb, hsub.trans (subset_sUnion_of_mem htS)⟩

/-- The **upper-limit observer**: the reversed Sorgenfrey topology on `ℝ`. -/
def upperTop : TopologicalSpace ℝ where
  IsOpen := IsUpperOpen
  isOpen_univ := fun x _ => ⟨x - 1, by linarith, by simp⟩
  isOpen_inter := by
    intro s t hs ht x hx
    obtain ⟨a1, ha1, hsub1⟩ := hs x hx.1
    obtain ⟨a2, ha2, hsub2⟩ := ht x hx.2
    exact ⟨max a1 a2, max_lt ha1 ha2, fun y hy =>
      ⟨hsub1 ⟨lt_of_le_of_lt (le_max_left _ _) hy.1, hy.2⟩,
       hsub2 ⟨lt_of_le_of_lt (le_max_right _ _) hy.1, hy.2⟩⟩⟩
  isOpen_sUnion := by
    intro S hS x hx
    obtain ⟨t, htS, hxt⟩ := hx
    obtain ⟨a, ha, hsub⟩ := hS t htS x hxt
    exact ⟨a, ha, hsub.trans (subset_sUnion_of_mem htS)⟩

/-- **Agreement characterization.**  A subset of `ℝ` is open in the standard
(Euclidean) topology iff it is open for *both* the lower- and upper-limit observers.
The forward direction shrinks a metric ball to a one-sided ray on each side; the
reverse direction glues a left ray `(a, x]` and a right ray `[x, b)` into the
two-sided ball `(a, b)`. -/
theorem isOpen_iff_lower_upper {U : Set ℝ} :
    IsOpen U ↔ IsLowerOpen U ∧ IsUpperOpen U := by
  constructor
  · intro hU
    rw [Metric.isOpen_iff] at hU
    refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
    · intro x hx
      obtain ⟨ε, hε, hball⟩ := hU x hx
      refine ⟨x + ε, by linarith, fun y hy => hball ?_⟩
      rw [Real.ball_eq_Ioo]; exact ⟨by linarith [hy.1], by linarith [hy.2]⟩
    · intro x hx
      obtain ⟨ε, hε, hball⟩ := hU x hx
      refine ⟨x - ε, by linarith, fun y hy => hball ?_⟩
      rw [Real.ball_eq_Ioo]; exact ⟨by linarith [hy.1], by linarith [hy.2]⟩
  · rintro ⟨hL, hU⟩
    rw [Metric.isOpen_iff]
    intro x hx
    obtain ⟨b, hb, hLsub⟩ := hL x hx
    obtain ⟨a, ha, hUsub⟩ := hU x hx
    refine ⟨min (b - x) (x - a), lt_min (by linarith) (by linarith), fun y hy => ?_⟩
    rw [Real.ball_eq_Ioo] at hy
    rcases le_total y x with h | h
    · apply hUsub
      refine ⟨?_, h⟩
      have : x - (x - a) ≤ x - min (b - x) (x - a) := by gcongr; exact min_le_right _ _
      linarith [hy.1]
    · apply hLsub
      refine ⟨h, ?_⟩
      have : x + min (b - x) (x - a) ≤ x + (b - x) := by gcongr; exact min_le_left _ _
      linarith [hy.2]

/-- **Flagship theorem.**  The standard topology on `ℝ` is the *agreement*
(supremum in the lattice of topologies, i.e. the sets open in both) of the
lower-limit and upper-limit topologies: two observers determine the Euclidean line. -/
theorem standard_eq_lower_sup_upper :
    (inferInstance : TopologicalSpace ℝ) = lowerTop ⊔ upperTop := by
  ext U
  rw [isOpen_iff_lower_upper]
  exact (@isOpen_sup ℝ lowerTop upperTop U).symm

/-! ### Non-degeneracy witnesses -/

/-- `[0, 1)` is open for the lower-limit observer. -/
theorem isLowerOpen_Ico01 : IsLowerOpen (Set.Ico 0 1) :=
  fun _ hx => ⟨1, hx.2, fun _ hy => ⟨le_trans hx.1 hy.1, hy.2⟩⟩

/-- `[0, 1)` is *not* open for the upper-limit observer (no `(a, 0]` fits inside it). -/
theorem not_isUpperOpen_Ico01 : ¬ IsUpperOpen (Set.Ico (0:ℝ) 1) := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨a, ha, hsub⟩ := h 0 ⟨le_refl 0, by norm_num⟩
  have h2 := hsub (⟨by linarith, by linarith⟩ : (a / 2) ∈ Set.Ioc a 0)
  exact absurd h2.1 (by simp; linarith)

/-- `(0, 1]` is open for the upper-limit observer. -/
theorem isUpperOpen_Ioc01 : IsUpperOpen (Set.Ioc 0 1) :=
  fun _ hx => ⟨0, hx.1, fun _ hy => ⟨hy.1, le_trans hy.2 hx.2⟩⟩

/-- `(0, 1]` is *not* open for the lower-limit observer (no `[1, b)` fits inside it). -/
theorem not_isLowerOpen_Ioc01 : ¬ IsLowerOpen (Set.Ioc (0:ℝ) 1) := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨b, hb, hsub⟩ := h 1 ⟨by norm_num, le_refl 1⟩
  have h3 := hsub (⟨by linarith, by linarith⟩ : ((1 + b) / 2) ∈ Set.Ico 1 b)
  exact absurd h3.2 (by simp; linarith)

/-- The lower-limit observer sees a topology **strictly finer** than the standard
line: `[0,1)` is open for it but not for the Euclidean topology. -/
theorem lowerTop_ne : lowerTop ≠ (inferInstance : TopologicalSpace ℝ) := by
  intro h
  have hop : IsOpen (Set.Ico (0:ℝ) 1) := by
    have : @IsOpen ℝ lowerTop (Set.Ico 0 1) := isLowerOpen_Ico01
    rwa [h] at this
  exact not_isUpperOpen_Ico01 (isOpen_iff_lower_upper.mp hop).2

/-- The upper-limit observer sees a topology strictly finer than the standard line. -/
theorem upperTop_ne : upperTop ≠ (inferInstance : TopologicalSpace ℝ) := by
  intro h
  have hop : IsOpen (Set.Ioc (0:ℝ) 1) := by
    have : @IsOpen ℝ upperTop (Set.Ioc 0 1) := isUpperOpen_Ioc01
    rwa [h] at this
  exact not_isLowerOpen_Ioc01 (isOpen_iff_lower_upper.mp hop).1

/-- The two observers are **incomparable**: neither topology refines the other.
`[0,1)` is lower- but not upper-open, so the two observers genuinely disagree. -/
theorem lowerTop_ne_upperTop : lowerTop ≠ upperTop := by
  intro h
  have : @IsOpen ℝ lowerTop (Set.Ico 0 1) := isLowerOpen_Ico01
  rw [h] at this
  exact not_isUpperOpen_Ico01 this

/-- The standard line is **not discrete** (`⊥` is the discrete topology, the bottom of
the lattice): the singleton `{0}` is not standard-open. -/
theorem standard_ne_bot : (inferInstance : TopologicalSpace ℝ) ≠ ⊥ := by
  intro h
  have hbot : @IsOpen ℝ ⊥ ({0} : Set ℝ) := trivial
  rw [← h] at hbot
  obtain ⟨b, hb, hsub⟩ := (isOpen_iff_lower_upper.mp hbot).1 0 rfl
  have := hsub (⟨by linarith, by linarith⟩ : (b / 2) ∈ Set.Ico 0 b)
  simp at this; linarith

/-! ### Phantom number of the real line -/

/-- **Two observers suffice.**  The pair `{lowerTop, upperTop}` is a genuine phantom
representation of the Euclidean line: their agreement is the standard topology and
each observer sees a strictly finer topology. -/
theorem isPhantomRep_real :
    IsPhantomRep (inferInstance : TopologicalSpace ℝ) {lowerTop, upperTop} := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · rw [sSup_pair]; exact standard_eq_lower_sup_upper.symm
  · intro t ht
    rcases ht with h | h
    · subst h; exact lowerTop_ne
    · rw [Set.mem_singleton_iff] at h; subst h; exact upperTop_ne

/-- **Phantom number of `ℝ` is exactly two.**  There is a two-observer phantom
representation of the standard line, and every phantom representation of it needs at
least two observers. -/
theorem real_phantom_number_eq_two :
    ∃ S : Finset (TopologicalSpace ℝ),
      IsPhantomRep (inferInstance : TopologicalSpace ℝ) (↑S) ∧ S.card = 2 ∧
      ∀ T : Finset (TopologicalSpace ℝ),
        IsPhantomRep (inferInstance : TopologicalSpace ℝ) (↑T) → 2 ≤ T.card := by
  classical
  refine ⟨{lowerTop, upperTop}, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · have hcoe : (↑({lowerTop, upperTop} : Finset (TopologicalSpace ℝ)) :
        Set (TopologicalSpace ℝ)) = {lowerTop, upperTop} := by simp
    rw [hcoe]; exact isPhantomRep_real
  · rw [Finset.card_pair lowerTop_ne_upperTop]
  · intro T hT; exact phantom_card_ge_two _ T hT standard_ne_bot

end PhantomTopology

import Mathlib

/-! # Topos-Theoretic Machine Learning: Foundational Definitions

This file collects the foundational definitions shared by the topos-theoretic
machine-learning bridge (`Bridges.VCCompactness`).  It fixes the vocabulary that
connects three domains:

* **Combinatorial learning theory** — concept families, shattering, VC dimension,
  the Sauer–Shelah growth bound, and PAC sample complexity.
* **Category theory / topos theory** — sieves on an object of a preorder and their
  lattice structure, together with the notion of *compact rank* (the categorical
  avatar of finite VC dimension).
* **Cryptography** — a hardness witness recording an explicitly shattered set.

Everything here is elementary; the mathematical content lives in
`Bridges.VCCompactness`.  The definitions are deliberately lightweight so that the
downstream file can state and prove the bridge theorems.
-/

open Finset Real

noncomputable section

/-! ## Concept families, shattering and VC dimension -/

/-- A **concept family** on `α` is a nonempty set of concepts (subsets of `α`). -/
structure ConceptFamily (α : Type*) where
  /-- The underlying set of concepts. -/
  concepts : Set (Set α)
  /-- A concept family is required to be nonempty. -/
  nonempty : concepts.Nonempty

/-- `C` **shatters** a finite set `S` if every subset `T ⊆ S` is cut out of `S`
by some concept of `C`. -/
def ConceptFamily.shatters {α : Type*} (C : ConceptFamily α) (S : Finset α) : Prop :=
  ∀ T : Finset α, T ⊆ S → ∃ c ∈ C.concepts, ∀ x ∈ S, (x ∈ c ↔ x ∈ T)

/-- `C.vcDimBound d` says the VC dimension of `C` is at most `d`: no shattered set
has more than `d` points. -/
def ConceptFamily.vcDimBound {α : Type*} (C : ConceptFamily α) (d : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ S : Finset α, C.shatters S → S.card ≤ d

/-- The **compact rank** of a concept family: `n` bounds every shattered set and is
either `0` or is itself realized by a shattered set of size `n`.  This is the
topos-theoretic avatar of "VC dimension equals `n`". -/
def CompactRank {α : Type*} (C : ConceptFamily α) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ S : Finset α, C.shatters S → S.card ≤ n) ∧
    (n = 0 ∨ ∃ S : Finset α, C.shatters S ∧ S.card = n)

/-! ## The Sauer–Shelah growth bound -/

/-- The **Sauer–Shelah bound** `∑_{i ≤ d} C(m, i)` on the growth function of a
family of VC dimension `d` restricted to a set of `m` points. -/
def sauerShelahBound (m d : ℕ) : ℕ := ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (d + 1), m.choose i

/-- At full dimension the Sauer–Shelah bound is `2^k`: everything is shattered. -/
theorem sauerShelah_full (k : ℕ) : sauerShelahBound k k = 2 ^ k := by
  unfold sauerShelahBound
  exact Nat.sum_range_choose k

/-! ## A cryptographic hardness witness -/

/-- A **hardness witness** at level `k`: an explicit shattered set of size `k`,
certifying that learning `C` requires resolving `k` independent bits. -/
structure CryptoHardnessWitness {α : Type*} (C : ConceptFamily α) (k : ℕ) where
  /-- The witnessing set. -/
  witness : Finset α
  /-- The witnessing set is shattered by `C`. -/
  witness_shattered : C.shatters witness
  /-- The witnessing set has exactly `k` points. -/
  witness_card : witness.card = k

/-! ## Transfer morphisms and PAC sample complexity -/

/-- A **transfer morphism** between concept families, recording the Lipschitz
constant governing how sample complexity inflates under transfer. -/
structure TransferMorphism {α β : Type*} (C₁ : ConceptFamily α) (C₂ : ConceptFamily β) where
  /-- The Lipschitz constant of the transfer. -/
  lipschitzConst : ℝ

/-- A PAC-style **sample complexity bound**: proportional to the VC dimension `d`,
inversely proportional to `ε²`, and logarithmic in the confidence `1/δ`. -/
def sampleComplexityBound (d : ℕ) (ε δ : ℝ) : ℝ := (d : ℝ) / ε ^ 2 * Real.log (1 / δ)

/-- Sample complexity is strictly positive for valid PAC parameters. -/
theorem sampleComplexityBound_pos {d : ℕ} {ε δ : ℝ}
    (hd : 0 < d) (hε : 0 < ε) (hδ : 0 < δ) (hδ1 : δ < 1) :
    0 < sampleComplexityBound d ε δ := by
  unfold sampleComplexityBound
  have hlog : 0 < Real.log (1 / δ) := Real.log_pos ((one_lt_div hδ).mpr hδ1)
  have hd' : (0 : ℝ) < d := by exact_mod_cast hd
  have hε2 : 0 < ε ^ 2 := by positivity
  exact mul_pos (div_pos hd' hε2) hlog

/-- Sample complexity is monotone in the VC dimension. -/
theorem sampleComplexity_linear_in_d {d₁ d₂ : ℕ} {ε δ : ℝ}
    (hε : 0 < ε) (hδ : 0 < δ) (hδ1 : δ < 1) (hd : d₁ ≤ d₂) :
    sampleComplexityBound d₁ ε δ ≤ sampleComplexityBound d₂ ε δ := by
  unfold sampleComplexityBound
  have hlog : 0 < Real.log (1 / δ) := Real.log_pos ((one_lt_div hδ).mpr hδ1)
  have hε2 : 0 < ε ^ 2 := by positivity
  have hcast : (d₁ : ℝ) ≤ d₂ := by exact_mod_cast hd
  gcongr

/-! ## Sieves on a preorder object and their lattice -/

/-- A **sieve** on `d` in a preorder `α`: a downward-closed set of objects below
`d`.  This is the elementary shadow of a sieve in a presheaf topos. -/
structure SieveOn (α : Type*) [Preorder α] (d : α) where
  /-- The underlying set of the sieve. -/
  carrier : Set α
  /-- Sieves are downward closed. -/
  downward_closed : ∀ x y, x ∈ carrier → y ≤ x → y ∈ carrier
  /-- Every element of the sieve lies below the target `d`. -/
  below_target : ∀ x, x ∈ carrier → x ≤ d

/-- Sieves are ordered by inclusion of carriers, forming a partial order. -/
instance {α : Type*} [Preorder α] {d : α} : PartialOrder (SieveOn α d) where
  le s₁ s₂ := s₁.carrier ⊆ s₂.carrier
  le_refl s := subset_refl _
  le_trans a b c hab hbc := subset_trans hab hbc
  le_antisymm := by
    rintro ⟨c1, _, _⟩ ⟨c2, _, _⟩ hab hba
    have h : c1 = c2 := subset_antisymm hab hba
    subst h; rfl

/-- The empty sieve. -/
def SieveOn.empty {α : Type*} [Preorder α] (d : α) : SieveOn α d where
  carrier := ∅
  downward_closed := fun _ _ hx _ => absurd hx (by simp)
  below_target := fun _ hx => absurd hx (by simp)

/-- The empty sieve is the least sieve. -/
theorem SieveOn.empty_le {α : Type*} [Preorder α] (d : α) (s : SieveOn α d) :
    SieveOn.empty d ≤ s := Set.empty_subset _

/-- The maximal sieve on `d`: everything below `d`. -/
def SieveOn.maximal {α : Type*} [Preorder α] (d : α) : SieveOn α d where
  carrier := {x | x ≤ d}
  downward_closed := fun _ _ hx hyx => le_trans hyx hx
  below_target := fun _ hx => hx

/-- The maximal sieve is the greatest sieve. -/
theorem SieveOn.le_maximal {α : Type*} [Preorder α] (d : α) (s : SieveOn α d) :
    s ≤ SieveOn.maximal d := fun _ hx => s.below_target _ hx

end

# Computational / Logical Evidence — Phantom Topologies

## 1. The core gluing identity (small-case check)

The agreement of the lower-limit and upper-limit observers is driven by the interval
identity, for `a < x < b`:

```
(a, x] ∪ [x, b) = (a, b)
```

Concrete instance `a = -1, x = 0, b = 1`:
- `(-1, 0] = {y : -1 < y ≤ 0}`
- `[0, 1)  = {y : 0 ≤ y < 1}`
- union `= {y : -1 < y < 1} = (-1, 1)`  ✓ (the two pieces overlap exactly at `x = 0`).

Conversely, the ball `(x-ε, x+ε)` contains both `[x, x+ε)` and `(x-ε, x]`, so every
Euclidean-open set is open for each observer. These two directions are exactly the
two halves of `isOpen_iff_lower_upper`.

## 2. Non-degeneracy witnesses (counterexample hunt for "1 observer")

| set        | lower-open? | upper-open? | Euclidean-open? |
|------------|-------------|-------------|-----------------|
| `[0, 1)`   | yes         | **no**      | no              |
| `(0, 1]`   | **no**      | yes         | no              |
| `(0, 1)`   | yes         | yes         | yes             |
| `{0}`      | no          | no          | no              |

- `[0,1)` open for lower but not upper  ⇒ `lowerTop ≠ upperTop` and `lowerTop ≠` standard.
- `(0,1]` open for upper but not lower  ⇒ `upperTop ≠` standard.
- Hence the two observers are **incomparable** and each is **strictly finer** than the
  real line: neither observer alone reproduces the Euclidean topology, so the phantom
  number is `> 1`.

Phantom number `≥ 2` for any non-discrete space rests on two lattice identities:
- `sSup ∅ = ⊥` (the empty observer family "agrees on everything" = discrete topology);
- `sSup {t} = t` (a single observer only reproduces itself).

as a future direction. Every table entry and identity here is discharged in the Lean

## 1. The Zariski plane demands three witnesses

**Conjecture.** The Zariski topology on the affine plane cannot be reconstructed as
the agreement of any two strictly finer topologies; it requires at least three
"observer" topologies whose common open sets recover exactly the Zariski opens.

**The key insight is** that the real line splits cleanly into a *left* and a *right*
one-sided refinement because its closed sets are governed by a single linear order,
whereas the Zariski plane has closed sets (finite unions of algebraic curves) that
meet along zero-dimensional configurations no pair of one-directional refinements can
separate — a third, transverse observer is forced. **Why now?** The two-observer
decomposition of the line, together with a clean lattice-theoretic lower bound
(agreement = supremum in the lattice of topologies), gives for the first time a
precise, testable notion of "number of observers", turning a slogan about
observer-dependent geometry into a concrete extremal problem.

**Conjecture.** Every second-countable topology is the agreement of two strictly
finer topologies; i.e. the phantom number of any space with a countable base is at
most two.

**The key insight is** that a countable base can be two-colored so that each color
class generates a strictly finer topology, and the two color classes intersect back
to the original base — mirroring exactly how `[a,b)` and `(a,b]` intervals split the
Euclidean base of the line. **Why now?** The line is the prototypical second-countable
space and its phantom number is now pinned to exactly two; the natural next step is to
test whether this ceiling is a general feature of countable bases or an accident of
the order structure of the reals.

## 3. Non-metrizability as an observer obstruction

**Conjecture.** A space is metrizable if and only if its phantom number is at most
two; every genuinely non-metrizable space needs at least three observers to be
reconstructed as an agreement of strictly finer topologies.

**The key insight is** that a two-observer decomposition equips a space with two
comparable one-sided "quasi-metrics" whose symmetrization is an honest metric, so a
phantom number of two secretly encodes metrizability — and its failure is exactly the
obstruction to metrizing. **Why now?** With the metrizable line realized by two
observers and a robust lower-bound method in hand, the tantalizing possibility is a
brand-new metrization criterion phrased purely in terms of how many observers a space
admits.

**Conjecture.** The phantom number of a topology equals the minimum number of
elements strictly above it in the lattice of topologies whose meet is the topology
itself; in particular a topology has a finite phantom number if and only if it is the
meet of its upper covers, and topologies that are meet-irreducible in the lattice have
no finite phantom representation at all.

**The key insight is** that "observers agreeing on the real topology" is literally an
infimum computation in the (order-reversed) lattice of topologies, so the phantom
number is a purely order-theoretic quantity that can be studied with the machinery of
lattice covers and irreducibility. **Why now?** The general lower bound already proved
(no non-discrete space is a phantom of a single observer) is the first rung of this
ladder; recasting the whole invariant lattice-theoretically would make it computable
for finite spaces and connect it to well-understood combinatorial structures.

two, while profinite (Stone) spaces exhibit an unbounded phantom spectrum as their

be split by two complementary refinements keyed to a partition of the point set,
whereas a rich clopen algebra forces many mutually incomparable refinements before

opposite extremes of topological complexity — one minimal, one combinatorially
maximal — so measuring their phantom numbers would calibrate the invariant across the
whole spectrum and reveal whether "observer count" tracks metrizability, cardinality,
or clopen complexity.

Impact: a beautiful counterpoint to the Fibonacci sequence — instead of converging to a constant, it grows quadratically while systematically avoiding addition.

import Mathlib
import Applications.CusickSumOfDigits

open Nat

namespace NumericalMonsters

/-- The core relation of the bestiary: in base `b`, the digits of `x` together
with the digits of `y` form a permutation of the digits of the product `x*y`.
Vampire, werewolf, ghost and zombie numbers are all refinements of this. -/
def SharesAllDigits (b x y : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (Nat.digits b x ++ Nat.digits b y).Perm (Nat.digits b (x * y))

/-- **Casting-out-`(b-1)`s invariant.**  If `x` and `y` share all their digits
with the product `x*y` in base `b ≥ 2`, then `x + y ≡ x*y  [MOD b-1]`. -/
theorem sharesAllDigits_modEq (b x y : ℕ) (hb : 2 ≤ b) (h : SharesAllDigits b x y) :
    (x + y) ≡ (x * y) [MOD (b - 1)] := by
  have hsum : (Nat.digits b x ++ Nat.digits b y).sum = (Nat.digits b (x * y)).sum :=
    h.sum_eq
  rw [List.sum_append] at hsum
  rcases Nat.lt_or_ge b 3 with hb3 | hb3
  · interval_cases b
    · exact Nat.modEq_one
  · have hmod : b % (b - 1) = 1 := by
      rw [Nat.mod_eq_sub_mod (by omega), show b - (b - 1) = 1 by omega,
        Nat.mod_eq_of_lt (by omega)]
    have hx := Nat.modEq_digits_sum (b - 1) b hmod x
    have hy := Nat.modEq_digits_sum (b - 1) b hmod y
    have hxy := Nat.modEq_digits_sum (b - 1) b hmod (x * y)
    calc
      x + y ≡ (Nat.digits b x).sum + (Nat.digits b y).sum [MOD (b - 1)] :=
        Nat.ModEq.add hx hy
      _ = (Nat.digits b (x * y)).sum := hsum
      _ ≡ (x * y) [MOD (b - 1)] := hxy.symm

/-- Base-`10` specialisation: `x + y ≡ x*y  (mod 9)`. -/
theorem sharesAllDigits_modEq_nine (x y : ℕ) (h : SharesAllDigits 10 x y) :
    (x + y) ≡ (x * y) [MOD 9] :=
  sharesAllDigits_modEq 10 x y (by norm_num) h

/-- **`ZMod 9` unit identity.**  In base `10`, each fang minus one is a unit:
`(x - 1) * (y - 1) = 1` in `ZMod 9`. -/
theorem sharesAllDigits_unit_nine (x y : ℕ) (h : SharesAllDigits 10 x y) :
    ((x : ZMod 9) - 1) * ((y : ZMod 9) - 1) = 1 := by
  have h2 : ((x : ZMod 9) + y) = ((x : ZMod 9) * y) := by
    have := (ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff (x + y) (x * y) 9).mpr
      (sharesAllDigits_modEq_nine x y h)
    push_cast at this
    exact this
  linear_combination -h2

/-- **Arithmetic taboo.**  No fang of a base-`10` digit-sharing factorisation is
congruent to `1` modulo `3`: `x % 3 ≠ 1`. -/
theorem fang_not_one_mod_three (x y : ℕ) (h : SharesAllDigits 10 x y) :
    x % 3 ≠ 1 := by
  intro hx
  have hz := sharesAllDigits_unit_nine x y h
  set f := ZMod.castHom (show (3 : ℕ) ∣ 9 by norm_num) (ZMod 3) with hf
  have himg : (f ((x : ZMod 9) - 1)) * (f ((y : ZMod 9) - 1)) = 1 := by
    rw [← map_mul, hz, map_one]
  have hx3 : ((x : ZMod 3)) = 1 := by
    conv_lhs => rw [← ZMod.natCast_mod x 3]
    rw [hx]; norm_num
  have hzero : f ((x : ZMod 9) - 1) = 0 := by
    rw [map_sub, map_natCast, map_one, hx3, sub_self]
  rw [hzero, zero_mul] at himg
  exact zero_ne_one himg

/-- The taboo is symmetric: the other fang also avoids `1 (mod 3)`. -/
theorem fang_not_one_mod_three' (x y : ℕ) (h : SharesAllDigits 10 x y) :
    y % 3 ≠ 1 := by
  apply fang_not_one_mod_three y x
  unfold SharesAllDigits at h ⊢
  rw [mul_comm]
  exact (List.perm_append_comm.trans h)

/-! ### Bridge to the binary sum-of-digits theory (`CusickSumOfDigits`) -/

/-- Sharing all digits in base `2` means the binary digit sums add:
`s₂(x) + s₂(y) = s₂(x*y)`. -/
theorem s2_add_of_sharesAllDigits (x y : ℕ) (h : SharesAllDigits 2 x y) :
    CusickSumDigits.s2 x + CusickSumDigits.s2 y = CusickSumDigits.s2 (x * y) := by
  have hsum : (Nat.digits 2 x ++ Nat.digits 2 y).sum = (Nat.digits 2 (x * y)).sum :=
    h.sum_eq
  rw [List.sum_append] at hsum
  simpa [CusickSumDigits.s2] using hsum

/-- Multiplying by two just prepends a zero digit, so `s₂(2*m) = s₂(m)`. -/
theorem s2_double (m : ℕ) : CusickSumDigits.s2 (2 * m) = CusickSumDigits.s2 m := by
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos m with hm | hm
  · simp [hm, CusickSumDigits.s2]
  · have := Nat.digits_base_pow_mul (b := 2) (k := 1) (m := m) (by norm_num) hm
    simp only [pow_one] at this
    simp [CusickSumDigits.s2, this]

/-- Binary digit-sum recursion: `s₂(n) = n % 2 + s₂(n / 2)`. -/
theorem s2_rec (n : ℕ) : CusickSumDigits.s2 n = n % 2 + CusickSumDigits.s2 (n / 2) := by
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos n with hn | hn
  · simp [hn, CusickSumDigits.s2]
  · rw [CusickSumDigits.s2, Nat.digits_def' (b := 2) (by norm_num) hn]
    simp [CusickSumDigits.s2]

/-- **Submultiplicativity of the binary digit sum.**  `s₂(x*y) ≤ s₂(x)·s₂(y)`.
Built on `CusickSumDigits.s2_subadditive`. -/
theorem s2_submul (x y : ℕ) :
    CusickSumDigits.s2 (x * y) ≤ CusickSumDigits.s2 x * CusickSumDigits.s2 y := by
  induction y using Nat.strong_induction_on with
  | _ y ih =>
    rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos y with hy | hy
    · simp [hy, CusickSumDigits.s2]
    · have hq : y / 2 < y := Nat.div_lt_self hy (by norm_num)
      have key : CusickSumDigits.s2 y = y % 2 + CusickSumDigits.s2 (y / 2) := s2_rec y
      have hmul : x * y = 2 * (x * (y / 2)) + (y % 2) * x := by
        have hy2 : y = 2 * (y / 2) + y % 2 := by omega
        calc x * y = x * (2 * (y / 2) + y % 2) := by rw [← hy2]
          _ = 2 * (x * (y / 2)) + (y % 2) * x := by ring
      rcases Nat.mod_two_eq_zero_or_one y with h0 | h1
      · rw [hmul, h0]
        simp only [zero_mul, add_zero]
        rw [s2_double]
        calc CusickSumDigits.s2 (x * (y / 2))
              ≤ CusickSumDigits.s2 x * CusickSumDigits.s2 (y / 2) := ih _ hq
          _ ≤ CusickSumDigits.s2 x * CusickSumDigits.s2 y := by rw [key, h0]; simp
      · rw [hmul, h1]
        simp only [one_mul]
        calc CusickSumDigits.s2 (2 * (x * (y / 2)) + x)
              ≤ CusickSumDigits.s2 (2 * (x * (y / 2))) + CusickSumDigits.s2 x :=
                CusickSumDigits.s2_subadditive _ _
          _ = CusickSumDigits.s2 (x * (y / 2)) + CusickSumDigits.s2 x := by rw [s2_double]
          _ ≤ CusickSumDigits.s2 x * CusickSumDigits.s2 (y / 2) + CusickSumDigits.s2 x :=
                Nat.add_le_add_right (ih _ hq) _
          _ = CusickSumDigits.s2 x * (CusickSumDigits.s2 (y / 2) + 1) := by ring
          _ ≤ CusickSumDigits.s2 x * CusickSumDigits.s2 y := by rw [key, h1]; ring_nf; omega

/-- `s₂(n) ≥ 1` for `n ≥ 1`. -/
theorem s2_pos (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) : 1 ≤ CusickSumDigits.s2 n := by
  induction n using Nat.strong_induction_on with
  | _ n ih =>
    rw [s2_rec]
    rcases Nat.mod_two_eq_zero_or_one n with h0 | h1
    · have hd : n / 2 < n := Nat.div_lt_self (by omega) (by norm_num)
      have : 1 ≤ CusickSumDigits.s2 (n / 2) := ih _ hd (by omega)
      omega
    · omega

/-- **Cross-domain bridge: binary fangs avoid powers of two.**  If `x` and `y`
share all digits with their product in base `2` (with `x, y ≥ 1`), then neither
fang is a power of two: `2 ≤ s₂(x)`. -/
theorem binary_fang_not_power_of_two (x y : ℕ) (hx : 1 ≤ x) (hy : 1 ≤ y)
    (h : SharesAllDigits 2 x y) : 2 ≤ CusickSumDigits.s2 x := by
  have hadd := s2_add_of_sharesAllDigits x y h
  have hsub := s2_submul x y
  have hxpos := s2_pos x hx
  have hypos := s2_pos y hy
  -- `s₂x + s₂y = s₂(xy) ≤ s₂x·s₂y`, with `s₂x, s₂y ≥ 1`, forces `s₂x ≥ 2`.
  nlinarith [hadd, hsub, hxpos, hypos]

/-! ### Non-vacuity witnesses -/

/-- The smallest vampire number: `1260 = 21 * 60`, and its fangs share all
digits with it. -/
example : SharesAllDigits 10 21 60 := by unfold SharesAllDigits; decide

example : (21 : ℕ) % 3 ≠ 1 ∧ (60 : ℕ) % 3 ≠ 1 := by decide

/-- A genuine base-`2` digit-sharing pair: `7 * 25 = 175`. -/
example : SharesAllDigits 2 7 25 := by unfold SharesAllDigits; decide

end NumericalMonsters

**Conjecture.** For every base `b ≥ 3`, a factorisation `v = x·y` in which the

by infinitely many such factorisations.

The key insight is that "sharing all digits" conserves the digit sum, and digit
sum modulo `b-1` is the number itself modulo `b-1`; this turns a combinatorial
digit condition into a multiplicative unit equation in the ring of integers
modulo `b-1`. Why now? The forward implication is settled as a base-independent
conservation law, so the ground is prepared to attack the far richer converse —
an equidistribution statement about which unit classes vampire-like numbers
occupy as the base varies.

eliminated before any multiplication is performed.

The key insight is that the unit-group obstruction modulo 9 projects onto a clean
residue taboo modulo 3, converting an arithmetic identity into a counting bound

**Conjecture.** In base 2, any factorisation `v = x·y` whose factors jointly reuse

`s₂(x), s₂(y) ≥ 2`; moreover the number of binary monsters below `2^n` grows like

The key insight is that binary digit sum is submultiplicative — a shift by a power
of two leaves it unchanged, so multiplication cannot create more one-bits than the
product of the factors' one-bit counts. Why now? The submultiplicative floor is
established, ruling out the "thin" factors (powers of two); the next step is to
